item.title: Interior painter Omagh: what to tell your decorator before the job
item.description: What interior painter Omagh covers in the house: walls, ceilings, woodwork and stairs, and what to say if the plaster is new or a wall is damp.
item.content:encoded:
Interior painter Omagh means the work inside the house: the rooms, the woodwork, the ceilings and the stairs, not the outside walls. Martin Kelly is based in Omagh. MC Decorating paints and wallpapers houses and small businesses across County Tyrone and County Fermanagh. This note is what to name before he prices that inside work. It is not a price, and it is not a claim that one brief suits every house in the town. What to ask before you book anyone is in how to choose a painter and decorator in Omagh.

What an interior painter Omagh quote should name

Interior painting in Omagh is the rooms, the hall and the stairs. Say whether you want one room or the whole interior. They are different bookings. The interior painting page covers a single room and a house from the front door to the back bedroom, so name which of those you mean.

That same page sets out the work. Floors, furniture and fittings are covered before a tin is opened. Holes and cracks are filled and sanded, stains and bare filler are spot-primed, walls and ceilings go on in even coats, and doors, frames, skirting and banisters are cut in to a clean line. The room is left tidy. If a quote does not mention that preparation, ask. Filling and cutting in are the decorating.

The sentence that changes the job is which surfaces you want. Walls only is not the same as walls plus doors, skirting and the rail. Woodwork left yellow beside a fresh wall is why a room can still look half done. Stairs, spindles and the high wall over the flight take longer than a square bedroom, so name them at the start. The photographs on our work show stairwells, halls and living rooms. They are not labelled by town, they are not a list of clients, and they are not a promise that your house will match one of them.

Halls, kitchens and ceilings

Halls, stairs and landings are worth naming separately for an interior painter in Omagh, because they are the part of the house people see first, they take the knocks, and spindles and the high wall over the stairs take longer than a square bedroom. If there is wallpaper above a dado, woodwork that has gone yellow, or spindles without a clean finish, name each of those. Paper on that top half is wallpapering. It waits until the wall is sound, dry and flat. If you want paint on the panels and paper above them, say both. A note that only says “the hall” can mean the walls, or it can mean the walls, the rail and the paper.

For a kitchen, say whether you mean the walls and the woodwork around the units, or the doors as well. The interior painting page asks you to say so, because painting the doors is a different job from the walls around them. One kitchen in the gallery shows the walls painted and the oak units left as they were. The later photograph shows a white splashback where the tiles had been multicoloured. The caption describes that picture. It is not a separate tiling service. Grease above a cooker is worth mentioning. Kitchens and bathrooms need a finish you can wipe. You do not need to scrub the walls before you ask.

If a ceiling has old filler from an earlier patch, name it. Side light from a window shows every ridge the wall would have hidden. Ceiling and wall repairs fill cracks, holes and scarred plaster so the paint has a flat surface. That is making good for decoration. It is not a replaster of the house, and it is not a damp-proof course. If the plaster is soft, hollow or coming away, say so before anyone prices a colour onto it. Paint will not hold a failing ceiling together.

A house that has been lived in, or a first decoration

Painting the inside of a house in Omagh depends on the house. The Omagh page describes older terraces and semis through Campsie, Kevlin, the Hospital Road, the Dublin Road and the Gortin Road, and newer estates where the plaster is still moving and a first decoration is overdue. Say which sort of house you have, whether paper has to come off, and whether the woodwork has yellowed. A repaint of a lived-in room is a different note from a first coat on plaster that has not settled.

If the plaster is new, say so in the message. You do not need to fill or sand it yourself before you ask. Leave flaking woodwork where it is, and point it out. Do not strip paper unless that has already been agreed. What to move, and what not to take apart, is in how to prepare a room before the decorator arrives.

Finish, light, and a wall that should wait

Light across Tyrone and Fermanagh is flat for much of the year. A colour picked from a phone often looks duller on a north-facing wall than it did on the screen. If you are unsure, put a sample on the actual wall and look at it in the morning and again in the evening before the whole room is committed. Late autumn is a useful week for that check, because you are seeing the light the room has for most of the year.

The interior painting page names matt for walls, and a wipeable eggshell or satin for doors, skirting and banisters, because hands touch them. A dark colour going pale, or a water stain, takes a primer and more coats, and that belongs in the quote. If the paint is already bought, give the name of the tin and say whether you are supplying it. A lower figure with the paint left out is a different job.

A patch that is still damp is a reason to wait. Mould and condensation marks come back if the cause is still feeding them, and ordinary emulsion will not stop that. Read what to check before painting over mould or condensation if a ceiling has a ring or a corner has gone black. Interior work can go ahead when the house is heated and the surfaces are dry. A cold spare room, or a ceiling that is still clammy, is the case for waiting. The outside does not share that calendar. Exterior painting needs a dry week, and a wall that is still holding rain stays unpainted until it is dry. The rooms do not have to wait for that week.

Nothing on this site is a figure for your room. What changes a price, with published UK guides marked as guides rather than a quote from Martin, is in how much it costs to paint a room in Northern Ireland.

What to send

If you want an interior decorator in Omagh to paint and paper the rooms, name the surfaces. A mood board is not the brief. A house in Fintona, or further across Tyrone and Fermanagh, needs the place written down. The journey is part of the quote. It is not priced as if every house were a street in the town.

Name these, in ordinary words. The town, and whether the house is an older terrace or a newer estate. The rooms, and whether stairs, doors, skirting and ceilings are included. Whether any paper comes off, or one feature wall goes on. Kitchen doors only if you want those painted; otherwise say the walls and the woodwork around the units. Anything cracked, stained, newly plastered, or damp to the touch. A rough date, and anything that cannot be moved.

Photographs on WhatsApp show the height of the stairs and the state of the ceiling before he travels. Use the quote form, call 07907 588 541, or email martink.kelly@yahoo.co.uk. He comes back with a price for the work you described. There is no obligation, and there is no set menu of prices.

item.title: What to name for landlord painting and decorating Omagh
item.description: What landlord painting and decorating Omagh covers on a house between tenants: rooms, paper, preparation, the next tenant’s date, and outside work only when the wall is dry.
item.content:encoded:
Landlord painting and decorating Omagh is the work on a house between tenants, done to the same standard as a home. Martin Kelly is based in Omagh. MC Decorating paints and wallpapers houses and small businesses across County Tyrone and County Fermanagh. Rental turnarounds sit on the commercial decorating page with shops, offices, salons and takeaways: surfaces made good, an even finish, and the place left fit to use. This note is what to name before he prices a rental in the town. It is not a price. What to ask before you book anyone is in how to choose a painter and decorator in Omagh.

What landlord painting and decorating Omagh includes

The quote comes after he knows the rooms, the condition and the town. Say how many rooms, whether paper has to come off, and the date the next tenant is due. A date in the message is more useful than a hopeful one. A full interior is a different diary slot from a single room. There is no set menu of prices, and nothing on this site is a figure for that house.

The preparation is the same as a home. Hard-wearing finishes on doors, frames and the lower walls that take the knocks are how a rental turnaround is approached. Ceilings and scruffy patches are repaired before the colour goes on. Interior and exterior work are both possible where the building needs both. That is a conversation at the quote, not a promise that every premises can be done overnight. There is no list of client names. The photographs on our work are houses. They show the finish, they are not labelled by town, and they are not a roll of rentals.

Because he lives and works from Omagh, a bedroom, a cloakroom or a stairs is straightforward to price. Describe the rooms and he will tell you whether it is a short job or a week. A whole interior between tenants is still a different booking from one room.

Preparation you do not need to start

You do not need to fill cracks, strip paper, wash walls or buy dust sheets before you ask. That work is the decorating. On an interior painting job, floors, furniture and fittings are covered before a tin is opened. Holes and cracks are filled and sanded, stains are spot-primed, and doors, frames, skirting and banisters are cut in to a clean line. The room is left tidy.

Leave flaking woodwork where it is, and point it out. If paper has to come off, say so, and leave the stripping unless that has already been agreed. Old paper comes off only where the wall is dry. Damp paper stains and lets go. Wallpapering for a hall, a stairs or one feature wall waits until the wall is sound, dry and flat. Ceiling and wall repairs make cracks, holes and scarred plaster good for paint and paper. They are not a replaster, and they are not a damp-proof course. If a wall is wet, a new coat will not fix the cause, and paint will not hide mould that condensation is still feeding. Clear what you would mind getting a speck on, and say which furniture cannot be moved.

Rooms that take the knocks

The job that comes up most in Omagh is the hall, stairs and landing. It is the part every visitor sees, and it takes the knocks. Wallpaper above a dado, woodwork that has gone yellow, and spindles that have never had a clean finish are the usual brief. Spindles and the high wall over the stairs take longer than a square bedroom, so put them on the quote. Ceilings with old filler spots are common in town houses that have been patched. Newer estates, where the plaster is still moving, are the other side of the same town. Say which sort of house it is.

Matt is the usual choice for walls. A wipeable eggshell or satin is the usual choice for doors, skirting and banisters. Kitchens and bathrooms want a finish that can be cleaned. A dark colour going pale, or a water stain, takes a primer and more coats, and that belongs in the quote. If the paint is already bought, give the name of the tin.

Interior painting can go ahead when the house is heated and the surfaces are dry. A cold spare room, or a ceiling that is still clammy, is a reason to wait.

The outside, and a rental that is not in the town

Exterior work waits for a dry spell. On the edge of Omagh, towards the Sperrins, outside walls take more weather. If the wall is still holding rain, it does not get a coat that week. A wall can look dry at lunchtime and still be holding last night’s rain. Late spring through early autumn is the realistic window. Winter is often the wrong week. Exterior painting covers rendered walls, pebbledash, masonry, fascias, soffits, bargeboards, doors, windows and garden walls. Name which you want. “The outside” can mean the front door, or the whole shell.

He looks at the wall first, and he would rather wait than trap water in a wet or crumbling surface. If the timber has gone soft, paint will not restore it. He is a decorator, not a roofer. There are no exterior photographs in the gallery yet. What to name on a Fermanagh house, including one between tenants, is in what to name for exterior house painting Fermanagh. If the outside is only part of the job, all five kinds of work are on the services page.

Enniskillen is about forty minutes down the A32, on the island between the two loughs. Rental houses between tenants are a regular ask there too. If you have a date the keys have to be back, put it in the message. The quote includes that travel. It is not priced as if the house were a street in Omagh. Name the place either way.

What to send

Use the quote form, call 07907 588 541, email martink.kelly@yahoo.co.uk, or send photographs on WhatsApp. The form asks for the town, the type of job and a rough timescale. The message is for the rooms, whether paper comes off, anything that should be made good first, and the date the next tenant is due. He comes back with a price for the work you described. There is no obligation.

item.title: What to name for exterior house painting Fermanagh
item.description: What exterior house painting Fermanagh involves: render, pebbledash, fascias, doors and windows, and why a coat around the loughs waits for a dry week.
item.content:encoded:
Exterior house painting Fermanagh means the outside of the house: the walls, the wood and the doors, not a colour chosen from a chart indoors. Martin Kelly is based in Omagh. He paints the outside of houses and small commercial buildings across County Tyrone and County Fermanagh, and he takes work across the border when the job suits. This is what to name before anyone prices a Fermanagh house. It is not a price, and it is not a claim that every week is dry enough to paint.

What exterior house painting Fermanagh includes

On the exterior painting page the surfaces are rendered walls, pebbledash, masonry, fascias, soffits, bargeboards, doors, windows and garden walls. A note that only says “the outside” can mean the front door, or it can mean the whole shell. Name which of those you want, and say whether the old coat is peeling or only tired.

The order of the work does not change with the town. He looks at the wall first. Paint will not hold on a wet or crumbling surface, and he would rather wait than trap water in it. Washing down includes the green growth on shaded and north-facing walls. Loose paint is scraped, cracks are filled, and bare patches are primed. Render and pebbledash take a masonry paint suited to them. Exterior wood takes its own system. Paths, planting and glass are protected, and the place is left tidy.

Emulsion from a kitchen or a bedroom is not an outside paint. The Enniskillen page says the same of the lough shore: lake air is not a reason to put interior emulsion on an outside wall. The longer account of wet walls, algae and soft timber is exterior paint for damp Northern Ireland weather.

The towns, and why the journey is on the quote

Irvinestown is about twenty-five minutes from Omagh, the first Fermanagh town on the road to Enniskillen. It is not as exposed as the west shore of the lough, but north-facing render still grows green and peeling sills are common. Exterior coats there are booked for a dry week, not forced through a wet one. Ballinamallard is the river village on that same road, about half an hour from Omagh, and it is covered the same way.

Enniskillen is about forty minutes down the A32, through Irvinestown. The quote includes that travel. It is not priced as if the house were a street in Omagh. Render and older stone stay damp, algae sits on shaded walls, and a coat put on too soon fails. The outside work is planned around a dry spell, the same as on the Sperrin side of Tyrone.

Kesh is the village on the north shore of Lower Lough Erne, out through Ederney. It is about half an hour to forty minutes from Martin, depending on the townland. Gables face the lough, north walls go green, and fascia boards soften at the ends. If the timber has gone soft, paint will not restore it. He will point that out. Replacing rotten wood is a separate decision: he is a decorator, not a roofer. Masonry wants a breathable exterior paint, and only once the wall is actually dry.

Lisnaskea is the furthest town on the list, past Enniskillen towards Upper Lough Erne. Allow about an hour from Omagh. Exterior wood and render take the same lough weather, sometimes with fewer neighbours to shelter a gable. Peeling paint is scraped back. A fresh coat over flakes will not last the winter. A full house, a shop, or a place that has been waiting is the sort of job that makes the drive sensible. A tiny touch-up may not, and he would rather say so than book a day that does not work. Houses around Donagh and Maguiresbridge sit on the same edge of the round.

If the place is a village between those towns, name it. The areas pages are the main towns, not a closed list, and the journey is part of the quote either way.

When the week is the wrong week

Late spring through early autumn is the realistic window for outside work. Winter is often the wrong week even when the diary is free. Omagh sits under the Sperrins, and Enniskillen, Kesh and the lough shore stay damp. A wall can look dry at lunchtime and still be holding last night’s rain. A wet wall, a crumbling surface, frost on a fresh coat, or an active leak above the paint are reasons to wait.

You do not need to wash the walls, scrape the flakes or buy the masonry paint before you ask. That work is the decorating. Point out what is peeling, what is only faded, and any timber that feels soft.

Rooms do not share that calendar. Interior painting can go ahead when the house is heated and the surfaces are dry. A cold spare room is still a reason to wait. The outside waits on the weather either way.

What to send with the ask

Say the town, whether it is the walls, the woodwork, the doors, or all of it, and whether the old coat is peeling or just tired. Photographs on WhatsApp show the height and the condition before he travels. There are no exterior photographs in the gallery yet. The rooms on our work show the standard of finish, and exterior jobs go on the Facebook page when they are photographed.

A shop or another small premises is the same outside work, with the timing talked through so the place is not closed for longer than the job needs. That is set out on commercial decorating. It is a conversation at the quote, not a promise that every premises can be done overnight. A house between tenants should include the date the next person is due. All five kinds of work are listed on the services page if the outside is only part of the job.

Nothing on this site is a price for the house. Use the quote form, call 07907 588 541, email martink.kelly@yahoo.co.uk, or send the photographs on WhatsApp. Name the town and the surfaces. He will come back with a price for that work. There is no obligation, and there is no set menu of prices.

item.title: How to choose a painter and decorator in Omagh
item.description: What to ask before booking a painter and decorator in Omagh: written quotes, preparation, coats, materials, insurance and the Northern Ireland weather.
item.content:encoded:
Choosing a painter and decorator in Omagh starts with the written quote, not with whoever answered first. A recommendation or a page online can be a fair start. Neither says what the price includes. This is a homeowner’s guide to the questions worth asking before you book anyone. The Omagh page is separate: it is what MC Decorating does in the town, where Martin Kelly is based.

He paints and wallpapers houses and small businesses across County Tyrone and County Fermanagh, and across the border when the job suits. Ask him what you would ask anyone else. This is not a ranking, and it is not a price.

What to ask a painter and decorator in Omagh before you book

Ask for the quote in writing, with the rooms and the surfaces named. A single number is not something you can compare.

  • Preparation. Filling, sanding, priming stains, washing growth off an outside wall and scraping loose paint are what make a finish last. If that work is not on the quote, it is not in the price.
  • Number of coats. Ask how many are included, and whether a primer is allowed for when a dark colour is going pale or a stain might show through. Ordinary emulsion over a water stain lets the mark come back.
  • Paint brand and finish, chosen with you. Matt on walls, and a wipeable eggshell or satin on doors and skirting, is the usual split. Kitchens and bathrooms need a finish you can clean. Agree it before the job, or name the tin if you have already bought the paint.
  • Who supplies the materials. Say whether paint, filler and primer are in the price or left for you to buy. A lower figure with the materials excluded is a different job.
  • Timescales. Ask for a start, how many days, and what happens if rain or a damp patch stops the work. Stairs and landings take longer than a bedroom, so put them on the quote if they are part of it.
  • Tidy-up. Floors, furniture and fittings covered before a tin is opened, and the room left tidy. On a longer job, that includes the hall, because sanding dust travels.
  • Public liability insurance. Ask to see the certificate. A spoken yes is not the document. Ask anyone you might book, including Martin. This article does not state what cover he holds.

Also ask who will be in the house. A decorator in Omagh may work alone or bring someone else for a larger job. The quote should name who is responsible.

Getting quotes you can compare

Two painters in Omagh can both be capable and still price different jobs. One may have allowed for filling and woodwork. The other may have priced the walls only. The lower figure is not a saving until the descriptions match.

Give each person the same brief: the town, the rooms, whether paper comes off, whether woodwork is included, and anything cracked, stained or damp. If only one of them has visited, they have not seen the same thing.

How much it costs to paint a room in Northern Ireland sets out what changes a price, using published UK guides that are not an MC Decorating quote. There is no set price list on this site.

Tick preparation, coats, finish, who buys the materials, woodwork and time on each quote, and ask whether the figure includes VAT. Use that same list for a painter and decorator Co Tyrone. A house in Fintona, Strabane or further into Fermanagh needs the place name on the quote, because the journey is not a street in the town.

Interior and exterior timing in Northern Ireland weather

Inside and outside do not share a calendar. Winters here are mild and wet.

Interior painting can go ahead in a Tyrone winter when the house is heated and the surfaces are dry. A cold spare room, or a ceiling that is still clammy, is a reason to wait. Paint will not hide mould that condensation is still feeding. Mould and condensation before painting is how to tell that from a leak.

Exterior painting needs a dry surface and time for the coat to cure. Omagh sits under the Sperrins, and a wall can look dry at lunchtime while it still holds last night’s rain. Late spring through early autumn is the realistic window. Exterior paint for damp Northern Ireland weather covers when to leave a wall alone. If the quote says the outside work moves with the forecast, do not book a week that is already forecast wet.

What to have ready

You do not need to fill, strip or buy dust sheets before a price. That work is the decorating. Have the town, the rooms, a rough date, and whether paper is coming off. Point out a stain or a damp patch, and do not paint over it the night before.

Once you have booked, preparing a room before the decorator arrives covers what to move and what to leave. Name the tin if you have chosen a colour.

The words “house painter Omagh” on a van do not say whether ceilings and woodwork are included. Ask. A silent ceiling, or doors left out, is a different job.

Red flags

  • No written quote, or a price that will not say what is included.
  • Pressure to pay a large cash sum, or to book the same day, before you have read it.
  • A refusal to show public liability insurance when you ask to see the certificate.
  • Painting over mould, a wet patch or flaking render because the diary is free. Paint does not dry a wall or mend a leak.
  • A round figure with no preparation, coats or materials.
  • No name on the quote, so you cannot tell who is responsible.

A missing shopfront is not one of those flags. You want a name on the quote and a description you can compare.

How to choose, then ask for a price

Take the written quote that describes the same rooms, the same preparation and the same finish, from someone who will show an insurance certificate and name a start. The lowest number only wins when it is the same work, in Omagh or further across Tyrone and Fermanagh.

If you want Martin to price the job, use the quote form. Name the town, the rooms and roughly when you would like it done. Say whether paper, woodwork or the outside is included. He will come back with a price for that work. There is no obligation, and there is no set menu of prices on this site.

item.title: Mould and condensation marks: what to do before painting a ceiling or wall
item.description: Why mould and condensation marks on an interior ceiling or wall come back if you paint over them, and what to check first in a damp Omagh winter.
item.content:encoded:
Black marks on a bathroom ceiling, a grey bloom behind a wardrobe, and rings in a kitchen corner show up every winter in Omagh and across Tyrone and Fermanagh. The weather is mild and wet, windows stay shut, and cold outside walls never really warm through. Paint over the marks and they come back through the new coat, or the growth sits on top of it. This is about inside ceilings and walls. Wet outside walls are a different job, set out in exterior paint for damp Northern Ireland weather.

Martin paints interiors when the surface is dry and the cause has been dealt with.

Why a coat does not hide it

The mark is water, or growth on that water, not a colour a coat will hide. Ordinary emulsion lets staining through, so a ceiling that looked white on Saturday can show the ring again within a few weeks. Primer on a wet patch fails the same way: it blisters, or the stain returns when the room steams up. Cold ceilings, outside bedroom walls and the plaster above a shower stay cold when the house is left unheated. Paint does not warm them.

Condensation, or water getting in

Most winter marks in bathrooms, kitchens and bedrooms are condensation. Steam from showers, cooking and drying clothes lands on the coldest surface. It is usually condensation when the marks are in several cold places, the surface is dry to the touch by the afternoon, it eases when a window is opened, and no single patch is growing from one point.

A leak, penetrating damp or rising damp needs the right trade before a decorator starts.

  • A leak stays wet, or worsens after rain, a shower upstairs, or a pipe running. A ring from one spot, or a drip, is a plumber’s job, or a roofer’s if the water is coming through the roof.
  • Penetrating damp is rain getting through a gable, a chimney, a gutter or a sill. The patch follows the weather. Fix the outside fault before any inside coat.
  • Rising damp sits low on a ground-floor wall. Skirtings soften, plaster bubbles up from the floor, and there is often a tide mark. Emulsion will not stop it. A decorator does not install a damp-proof course.

Ceiling and wall repairs on this site are making good for decoration once the plaster is fit to paint, not a damp survey. If the mould covers a large area, or you are worried about health, ask your GP, your landlord, or environmental health.

Habits that keep the moisture down

  • Run the bathroom and kitchen fan during the steam and after you leave. A tissue at the grille should pull in. A fan blowing into the loft, not outside, only moves the damp.
  • Leave trickle vents open. Painting those slots shut, or covering them with curtains, blocks the air the windows were fitted to give.
  • Drying clothes in a shut bedroom loads that room with water. Open a window if you have to, keep wardrobes off the cold wall, and vent a tumble dryer outside.
  • Steady background heat keeps walls warmer than a cold house blasted for two hours at night.
  • Leave a gap behind furniture on an external wall. That stops the black patch in the shape of a headboard.

Clean it, and do not mix products

If a decorator is coming, say there is mould or a stain and leave the washing to the job. The note on preparing a room before the decorator arrives already says not to wash walls with something you would not put on your hands, and not to paint a damp patch the day before.

On a small patch of your own, wear gloves, open the window, and follow the label on a cleaner sold for mould on paint. Do not mix products. Bleach and another cleaner together can give off dangerous fumes in a bathroom. Wipe, rather than dry-sanding, and leave flaking paint so the plaster stays put.

Let it dry, then block the stain

In a Tyrone winter a bathroom ceiling can take days to dry. If it feels clammy, or the ring is still dark and damp, wait. Keep the room heated as usual and the steam down.

Water stains and the ghost of mould still show through ordinary emulsion, so a stain-blocking primer for interior walls and ceilings goes on the dry patch, then the finish. That is a type of product, not a brand tied to this work. It will not hold a stain while water is still getting in.

Paint that suits the room

A bathroom or kitchen wants an emulsion labelled for those rooms, moisture-resistant or mould-resistant. Bedroom matt on a shower ceiling stays damper and marks sooner. Other rooms can take a normal interior emulsion once the cause has gone. A mould-resistant tin resists growth on a clean, dry surface. It does not mend a leak, a blocked gutter or a fan that does not extract.

Ceilings show every tide mark, so they are where the primer earns its place. If the plaster is soft, hollow or coming away, stop. Interior painting is for a surface that can take paint. Where it cannot, ceiling and wall repairs come first.

When it is a decorator’s job

Clean and touch in a small dry patch yourself if you can reach it. Ask a decorator when the marks run across a ceiling, the paint is flaking, wallpaper has lifted, or you want the room finished after a leak has been repaired. Say which room, whether anything is still wet, and whether a plumber or roofer has already been.

Name the town, whether that is Omagh or further out in Enniskillen or Strabane. Use the quote form and send a photograph of the stain on WhatsApp. The colour can wait until the surface is dry.

item.title: How to prepare a room before the decorator arrives
item.description: What to move, what to leave alone, and what to tell the decorator before the first morning at a house in Omagh, Tyrone or Fermanagh.
item.content:encoded:
The useful preparation, before a decorator comes to a house in Omagh or elsewhere in Tyrone and Fermanagh, is ordinary household work. It is not filling cracks, stripping paper, or deciding whether a damp wall can take paint. Those belong to the job. This is how to leave the room so the first morning is spent on the walls.

Leave the walls to the decorating

Filling, sanding, priming stains, and stripping paper that is already failing are decorating, not a task to finish the night before. The order for paper is in how walls are prepared for wallpaper. Cracks and holes are ceiling and wall repairs. A wet outside wall is a different question, set out in exterior paint for damp Northern Ireland weather. You do not need to start any of that yourself.

Leave old paint where it is. Flaking woodwork in an older house in Omagh, Fintona or Enniskillen can be decades old. Do not sand it, burn it off, or scrape it back to bare wood. Dust and heat are not a head start, and a chemical stripper is the wrong thing to open in a bedroom. Point the woodwork out when you ask for the quote. Making it good is part of the decorating.

Clear what you care about, and what is in the way

Clear the surfaces of anything you would mind getting a speck on: photographs, ornaments, clocks, lamps, medicines, and paper on a windowsill. Curtains and blinds can stay. If you want them down so a frame can be painted, take them down only when the fittings lift off easily. Do not unscrew a pelmet or a blind that needs a ladder. Say it is still up.

Rugs, toy boxes, cables and small furniture come out of the room, or into the middle if that is the only space. A heavy wardrobe, a piano, a bed you cannot shift on your own, or a sofa that blocks the door should stay where it is. Do not drag it. Say what has to remain when you ask for a quote. Working around a piece of furniture is normal. Finding that out on the morning is what uses up the day.

Pictures and mirrors come down if you can lift them without a stretch you are unsure of. Leave the hooks. A hook pulled out of old plaster makes a bigger hole than the one already there, and filling is part of making the wall good. Fixed shelves stay unless they lift straight off.

What not to take apart

  • Do not remove sockets, switches, light fittings or radiators. A live fitting is not evening preparation.
  • Do not lift floorboards, move a boiler, or drain anything.
  • Do not wash the walls with bleach, or with a cleaner you would not put on your hands. A wall that is already dry and free of cobwebs is enough. If there is grease above a cooker, say so.
  • Do not put a coat of paint on yourself to save time. A soft new coat, or a tin that does not suit the surface, adds work.
  • Do not strip wallpaper unless that has already been agreed. Paper often brings plaster with it. If the paper is to come off, say so in the message. The wallpapering page is the work of hanging it once the wall is ready, not a reason to strip the house yourself the week before.

You do not need to buy dust sheets or mask the house. On the interior painting page, the work includes floors, furniture and fittings covered before a tin is opened, and the room left tidy at the end of the day. Clearing the clutter is the part that helps. Covering the room is the decorating.

The way in, and who is in the house

The hall is the way into the room, and in many of these houses the hall, stairs and landing are the job. Clear coats, shoes, prams and bags off the route from the door you want used. If the stairs are being painted, anything stored on the steps needs to move before the first morning.

Keep dogs and cats out of the room while paint is wet. A door left open for a cat is how hair gets into a finish. Keeping children out of that room is the same ordinary care. You do not need to empty the house. Do say if someone is sleeping in the next room, or if a dog will be loose in the hall.

Streets are often tight. Fintona’s own page says so of the village, and a space near the door helps on an older terrace in Omagh too, if you can leave one. It depends on the street. Name the town either way: Omagh, Strabane, Enniskillen, Irvinestown, Kesh, or a village in between. The same clearing applies in each of them.

Heat, fresh air, and a wet patch

In the colder months a spare room is often the one left unheated. If the heating is already on in the house, leave that room on the same setting as the rooms you live in. Do not stand a gas heater or a borrowed stove in a closed bedroom to hurry it along. Do not light an open fire or a stove hard against a wall that is about to be painted. A window that opens is enough air. Shut it if the house will be empty.

If a patch is cold, stained or wet to the touch, do not seal it with your own paint the day before, and do not expect paper over it in the morning. That includes a ground-floor wall in an older house, the sort of caution already noted for places such as Ballinamallard. Show the patch. Paint and paper do not fix a leak. The repairs page is plain about the limit: this is making good for decoration, not a damp-proof course.

Choose the colour before the morning

Winter light in Tyrone and Fermanagh is flat. A colour that looked right on a phone often dies on a north-facing wall in Omagh or Enniskillen. If you are unsure, put a sample on the actual wall and look at it in daylight and again with the lights on. The interior painting page says the same, because the choice is yours before the room is committed.

If you have already bought the paint, give the name. If you have not, say which rooms, and whether the doors, frames and skirting are included. A message that says “walls only” should mean walls only. Woodwork left undone is why a freshly painted room can still look tired.

Also say what is wrong with the surface: paper still on the wall, a ceiling with old filler, a stain, a dark colour going pale, or cracks over a door. What those things do to the work is in how much it costs to paint a room. This note does not add a price. Photographs of the room as it is, sent on WhatsApp, are more useful than a tidy picture of the fireplace.

What to put on the quote

The quote form asks for the town, the type of job and a rough timescale. The message is for the rooms, whether paper has to come off, and anything that should be made good first. A house in Lisnaskea or Cookstown needs the town written in. So does a street in Omagh.

A shop, an office or a house between tenants is a different sort of preparation. Say the opening hours, or the date the next tenant is due. That is what the commercial decorating page already asks for. Moving a sofa is the household version of the same idea: say what cannot be in the way.

On the morning, a clear path, the colour decided, pets out of the room, and a note of anything that has to stay will do. The walls are the decorating.

item.title: How much does it cost to paint a room in Northern Ireland?
item.description: What changes the price of painting a room in Tyrone or Fermanagh, with published UK guide figures clearly marked as guides rather than an MC Decorating quote.
item.content:encoded:
Martin does not publish a price list, and this article is not one. A room in Omagh, a stairs in Enniskillen and a damp gable in Kesh are different jobs. What follows is what actually changes a quote in Tyrone and Fermanagh, then two published UK guides so you can see the sort of figures that are circulating. Those figures are national ballparks. They are not a quote from MC Decorating, and they are not a Northern Ireland price index. London and the south-east pull UK averages up. A local price can sit differently, in either direction, once someone has seen the walls.

What changes the price

  • The room itself. A small bedroom with sound walls is a different day from a living room with a picture rail, a chimney breast and two colours.
  • Stairs, spindles and landings. They take longer than a square room of the same floor area. If they are in the job, say so at the start.
  • Preparation. Stripping wallpaper, filling cracks, sanding, and priming stains is often more of the labour than the final coat. A wall that looks “grand” until the paper comes off can change the job.
  • Condition. Nicotine, water stains, dark colours under a pale one, and fresh filler that has not been primed all add coats.
  • Woodwork. Doors, frames, skirting and banisters are a large share of a proper job. A quote for “walls only” will look cheaper and the room will still look tired.
  • How far it is from Omagh. A house in Lisnaskea or Cookstown is not the same call-out as a street in Omagh. The quote should be honest about that. There is no published call-out fee on this site, because it depends on the work.
  • The paint. Standard trade paint and a designer tin are not the same cost. If you have already bought a specific paint, say so.

Doing several rooms while the dust sheets are already down is usually better value than booking the same rooms months apart. That is about the setup, not a discount code.

Published UK guide figures

Checkatrade’s painter and decorator cost guide, in the detailed table marked as updated in October 2026, gives these UK-wide ballparks. The guide says they include regular trade paint and labour, and that premium paints cost more. A line of “fast facts” on the same page says a typical day rate of £325, while the table averages the day rate at £300. Treat that mismatch as a reason to use the guide loosely.

UK ballpark figures from the Checkatrade painter and decorator cost guide (table updated October 2026). These are not MC Decorating prices and they are not specific to Northern Ireland. Source: checkatrade.com.
Job in that guideFigure they publish
Day rate£250 to £350, average £300, before the table’s note on paint
Small room, about 8 square metres£350
Medium room, about 18 square metres£450
Large room, about 30 square metres£1,000
Hall, stairs and landing£1,450 to £1,750, average £1,600
Wallpapering a room, labour only£350 to £500. The paper itself is extra and varies a lot

Screwfix publishes a wider UK range in its own 2026 guide, on different assumptions: walls and ceilings, only minor preparation, and you move the furniture yourself. Their professional column is £200 to £450 for a small room, £250 to £600 for a medium room, and £350 to £900 for a large one. Source: Screwfix, how much to paint a room.

The gap between those two guides is the useful lesson. “The cost to paint a room” depends on what is included. A number with no description of prep, woodwork and paint is not a quote.

There is no separate Northern Ireland index here

I am not going to invent a Tyrone or Fermanagh average to sit beside those UK figures. Travel, the age of the houses, and how long walls stay damp all change the work, especially on exteriors. For outside paint, the limitation is often the weather rather than the price of the tin. That is covered in exterior paint for damp Northern Ireland weather.

What to tell Martin

On the quote form, the useful details are the town, the rooms, whether paper has to come off, and roughly when you want it done. Photographs on WhatsApp help if the walls are cracked or the stairs are part of it. He will come back with a price for that job. If you are comparing it with a UK guide, compare it with a description, not with a single average.

Interior work is set out on the interior painting page. Paper is separate, because the material is yours to choose: wallpapering.

item.title: Exterior paint for damp Northern Ireland weather
item.description: How to think about exterior paint in Tyrone and Fermanagh: wet walls, algae, render, pebbledash and timber, and when a wall should not be painted yet.
item.content:encoded:
Outside paint in Tyrone and Fermanagh fails for dull reasons. The wall was still damp. The green film was painted over. Flaking paint was coated rather than scraped off. Or a product meant for a living room went onto render because it was the tin in the shed. The climate is wet, the Sperrins and the loughs keep surfaces damp, and a “dry day” in the forecast is not the same as a dry wall.

Martin paints exteriors when the surface is fit and the week will let the coat cure. This is what is worth knowing before you ask for that quote. It is not a product advertisement, and it does not name a brand he is tied to.

Do not paint a wet wall

Render, pebbledash and older solid walls take up rain and let it out slowly. If you seal a wet wall with a film that cannot breathe, the moisture stays behind the paint. The coat blisters, or the damp finds another way out indoors. A breathable masonry paint, sold for exterior render and pebbledash, is the usual specification for those walls. Emulsion from a kitchen or bedroom is not an outside paint, even if the colour is right.

A wall can feel cold and look dry while the core is still wet, especially on the north side, under trees, or on a gable facing Lower Lough Erne or the hills above Gortin and Newtownstewart. If it is wet to the touch, or an older stain is still active, the job waits. Painting it that afternoon does not make you further on.

Green walls need cleaning first

Algae and mould sit on shaded render all over the counties. Paint on top of them does not kill the growth. It comes through, or the new coat lets go. The sequence is wash, treat, let it dry, then paint. North-facing walls and anything under a dripping tree are the usual places. This is ordinary prep, and it belongs in the quote.

Scrape what is already failing

Flaking and chalking paint has lost its grip. A new coat sticks to the flake, and the flake is what falls off. Loose material comes off, bare patches are primed, and cracks are filled before the finish. If you can pull ribbons of old paint off with a scraper, that is the job, not a quick freshen-up.

Timber is a different problem

Fascias, soffits, bargeboards, sills and doors fail at the joints, where water sits. If the wood is soft under a knife, paint will not restore it. The rotten piece needs repaired or replaced first, or you will be painting it again next year. Martin will point that out. Replacing roof timber is not the decorating, and he will not pretend a coat of gloss is a repair.

Windows should be painted so the edges that meet the frame are covered, and they should not be painted shut. Open them while the work is done. It is a small thing and it is how sashes and modern casements end up stuck.

When he will not paint

  • The wall is wet, or there is an active leak above it
  • Frost is due on a fresh coat
  • The surface is crumbling in handfuls rather than holding a coat
  • The only available day is in the middle of a wet fortnight

Late spring to early autumn is the realistic season. Even then, a job moves if the weather turns. That is normal in Omagh, Enniskillen, Kesh and the glen. It is not a decorator being awkward.

Colour is the last decision

Very dark masonry on a sunny gable runs hotter and can fade sooner. In this climate the bigger risk is still moisture, not the sun. Choose a colour you can live with on a grey day, because that is most days. Look at it on the actual wall if you can, not only on a chart indoors.

Published UK price guides do include exterior averages. They are national figures with their own assumptions, and they are not a quote for your house. The cost article explains how to read them. For the work itself, see exterior painting, or ask Martin for a quote with the town, what needs painted, and whether it is peeling or only faded. Photos on WhatsApp are the fastest way to show a gable.

item.title: Wallpaper going up in local houses, and how to prep the walls
item.description: Floral cloakrooms, marble-effect halls and a single feature wall: how walls are prepared so new wallpaper holds in a damp Northern Irish house.
item.content:encoded:
The patterns in Martin’s recent photographs are a better guide to what is going up locally than a shop’s “trend” wall. They are real rooms in ordinary houses: a dark floral downstairs toilet, a willow-leaf feature wall in a bedroom, marble-effect paper in a hall, botanicals above sage panelling on a stairs, leaf paper over a painted dado, and an art-deco fan paper in a living room. None of that is a claim about what the whole of Northern Ireland is buying. It is what he has actually been asked to hang.

What those jobs have in common

Small rooms can take a loud paper. The cloakroom with the burgundy and pink floral works because the room is tiny and the daylight is limited. The same paper across an open living room would be a lot. If you like a maximal pattern, a downstairs toilet or a short stretch of hall is the low-risk place.

One wall is often enough. The willow-leaf bedroom leaves the other walls painted. The dining room with the animal-portrait paper paints the return wall a dusky pink. The pattern does the work. The paint gives the eye a rest and keeps the cost of the paper down, because you are not buying it for every wall.

Halls are being split in half. Floral stripes, mottled papers and stone effects are going above panelling or a painted dado, not from skirting to ceiling. The lower wall takes the knocks from bags and children. Paint on that half can be washed. The paper stays at eye level, which is where you notice a hallway.

Stairs need a paper that can turn a corner. Large repeats and fake stone veins show every seam that drifts. A busy botanical can hide a slight mismatch better than a stripe. Either way, a stairs uses more paper than the floor area suggests, because the drops are long.

Prep, in the order that matters

  1. Check for damp. If the wall is wet, stop. Paper hides the mark and then stains or peels. Martin is not there to cover a leak with a floral. The cause needs dealing with first. He does not install damp-proof courses.
  2. Strip what is failing. Papering over paper is how bubbles and peeling edges start. The leaf-pattern job in the gallery shows the scarred plaster that can be waiting underneath. That gets filled before anything is hung.
  3. Fill and sand. A pattern will not disguise a lump. Side light on a landing shows it. Repairs are part of making the wall good, and they are easier before the paper is up than after.
  4. Size or line a patchy wall. Bare filler, old plaster and new skim drink paste at different rates. A sealer or a lining paper gives the finish a flatter base, especially under a pale or lightly textured design. A heavy pattern is more forgiving, but it still wants a sound wall.
  5. Same batch. Rolls bought later can differ even with the same name on the label. Order enough for the stairs and the mistakes. A spare roll is cheaper than a seam in a different shade halfway up the hall.
  6. Sockets and switches. Plates come off so the paper runs behind them, then go back. The power is off while that is done. It is part of the job, not a finishing shortcut of paper cut roughly around the plate.
  7. Match the pattern on purpose. Stripes, florals and stone effects need the repeat lined up. On a stairs the waste is in those matches. A “free match” paper is more economical. Ask before you fall for a large drop that will halve the useful length of each roll.

Choosing between paper and paint

Paint is the simpler finish on a wall that is slightly out of true, and it is easier to refresh in five years. Paper is the finish when you want the room to have a design you cannot get from a tin. Many of the houses in the gallery use both: paper where it earns its place, paint on the panels, the chimney breast, the woodwork and the ceiling.

The photographs are on our work, and the service is described on the wallpapering page. If you already have the rolls, say so when you ask for a quote, and say whether the old paper is still on the wall. That is the difference between a hang and a strip-and-hang.
